title: Get Good at Operating Systems in Six Weeks
audience: Developers who know how to write a program but want to understand processes, memory, scheduling, synchronization, and persistence well enough to debug and discuss real systems.
summary: Learn OS concepts through observations and small programs. Organize the subject around virtualization, concurrency, and persistence: how programs receive CPU and memory, how work overlaps safely, and how state survives failures. A Linux VM or WSL environment is enough for most introductory experiments.
outcomes: Explain process, thread, address-space, and system-call boundaries.
Reason about virtual memory, page faults, scheduling, and blocking I/O.
Identify race conditions and choose an appropriate synchronization primitive.
Distinguish a successful write from a documented durability guarantee.
foundations: Mechanism versus policy

A context switch saves and restores execution state; a scheduler chooses which runnable work executes. Page tables translate addresses; replacement policy chooses what to evict. Distinguishing mechanism from policy makes unfamiliar implementations easier to reason about.
Isolation and sharing

Processes normally have separate virtual address spaces, while threads within a process share memory and many resources. A shared address space makes communication cheap but also creates synchronization and lifetime hazards. Threads still have separate execution state and stacks.
Observe before theorizing

Use process listings, resource monitors, a debugger, and system-call tracing on your own programs. Predict whether a workload is running, blocked, or waiting for memory, then compare the prediction with evidence. Do not assume high elapsed time means high CPU use.
studyRule: Read one concept, implement a tiny experiment, predict the outcome, then explain any mismatch. Keep source code and observations together. Use only local programs and disposable files; OS learning does not require probing production machines.
plan: Week 1
Processes and execution

Study user/kernel mode, system calls, process creation, exit, and basic scheduling. Run a CPU-heavy loop and an I/O-waiting program, comparing elapsed and CPU time. Learn how file descriptors are owned and closed.
A process-state sketch and two measurements explaining why elapsed and CPU time differ.
Week 2
Virtual memory

Study address spaces, paging, translation, page faults, locality, and the difference between virtual and resident memory. Allocate memory, touch it gradually, and observe changes without exhausting the host.
A bounded experiment showing that reserving address space and physically touching pages are different events.
Weeks 3-4
Threads and coordination

Implement a shared counter and a bounded producer-consumer queue. Study mutexes, condition variables, deadlock, and safe shutdown. Explain the predicate protected by each lock and why waiting requires a loop.
A queue that does not lose work, exceed capacity, or leave a worker blocked after shutdown.
Weeks 5-6
Files and recovery

Learn page cache, filesystems, journaling, write ordering, and explicit sync operations. Study a temporary-file replacement pattern, its platform assumptions, and crash states. Review all concepts using one service's request path.
A persistence diagram and an explanation of what the application can promise after each successful call.

lab.title: Diagnose a slow worker without guessing
lab.scenario: A local worker takes five seconds to finish a request but uses very little CPU. You need to distinguish computation, waiting on a lock, sleeping, and waiting for a file or network dependency.
steps: Measure wall-clock and CPU time over a repeatable workload. Inspect the process and its threads while the delay occurs. Low CPU does not identify the cause, but it argues against optimizing arithmetic first.

Collect a stack trace or system-call trace from the process you own. Look for the actual blocking boundary: a wait primitive, read, connection operation, or deliberate sleep. Preserve timestamps and avoid logging sensitive inputs.

Change one controlled condition, such as removing a test sleep or replacing a slow local dependency with a fast stub. Repeat the measurement and check whether the observed wait disappears without changing the result.
lab.result: You can explain the latency using a measured blocking path rather than a vague claim that the OS is slow. The distinction guides whether to optimize computation, dependency behavior, or synchronization.
checks: Is the workload identical between comparisons?
Do stack or trace observations support the proposed bottleneck?
Does the change preserve correctness and avoid unbounded concurrency?
lab.extension: Run two workers sharing a lock and deliberately hold it during slow I/O. Measure how one blocked operation delays unrelated work, then reduce the critical section and compare throughput and latency.

qa: Is a thread always faster than a process?

No. Threads can reduce communication and creation overhead, but introduce shared-state risks and can contend on locks. The right choice depends on isolation, workload, runtime, and failure boundaries, not a universal speed rule.
Does a page fault always mean disk I/O?

No. Some faults allocate a new page or establish an existing mapping without disk access. Others require fetching data. Explain the fault type and backing state before concluding that storage is the bottleneck.
Does write success guarantee persistence?

Not necessarily. Data may be buffered in the application, kernel, or device. A durability claim depends on the API, synchronization, filesystem, and hardware contract; a generic successful write is not enough.
pitfalls: Memorizing definitions without tracing a real program.
Using volatile as a substitute for synchronization.
Claiming durability without identifying the persistence boundary.
readiness: A process and thread can be compared using resource ownership.
A page fault and context switch can be explained separately.
A queue has a safe wait predicate and shutdown path.
A file update has explicit crash and durability assumptions.

title: Plan Your Computer Networks Preparation
audience: Software engineers who need to understand request paths, transport behavior, naming, routing, and network failures rather than memorize protocol acronyms.
summary: Follow data from an application message to a remote service and back. Learn addresses, ports, routing, DNS, TCP/UDP, TLS, and HTTP through local experiments. Keep transport guarantees distinct from application guarantees: successful delivery of bytes does not prove a business operation completed once.
outcomes: Explain where naming, routing, transport, security, and application semantics fit.
Distinguish connection failure, timeout, reset, and application-level rejection.
Reason about bandwidth, latency, flow control, congestion, and connection reuse.
Use authorized packet or request inspection to test a network hypothesis.
foundations: Layers answer different questions

IP routes packets; transport protocols connect endpoints or deliver datagrams; TLS protects a channel; HTTP defines request semantics. A DNS name, IP address, port, and URL are related but not interchangeable. Debug the boundary that actually failed.
TCP is a byte stream

TCP provides ordered reliable bytes within a connection, not application message boundaries. Reads can return partial data or combine writes. Applications need framing, limits, and handling for disconnects while a message is incomplete.
Latency is not bandwidth

A fast link can still have high round-trip delay. Connection setup, DNS, TLS, server queueing, and payload transfer contribute differently. Flow control protects a receiver; congestion control responds to network capacity. Neither removes the need for bounded application queues.
studyRule: Use a local client and server you control. Predict a request trace, introduce one safe delay or disconnect, and compare the result. Capture only authorized traffic and avoid storing credentials, private payloads, or other people's communications.
plan: Week 1
Addressing and delivery

Study IP addresses, subnets, routes, ports, sockets, and local versus remote destinations. Inspect your own machine's interfaces and routes. Draw the path to a local service and explain which component chooses the next hop.
A labeled path diagram and a client that connects to an explicitly chosen local endpoint.
Week 2
Transport semantics

Implement a framed TCP exchange and compare it with a UDP datagram example. Test partial reads, disconnects, and timeouts. Learn handshakes, retransmission, ordering, flow control, and congestion at a conceptual level.
A parser that waits for a complete bounded message and does not assume one read equals one write.
Weeks 3-4
Web protocols

Study DNS resolution, TLS identity checks, HTTP methods, status codes, caching, and connection reuse. Compare browser timing with a command-line HTTP client. Learn that HTTP/3 uses QUIC rather than TCP.
A request timeline separating DNS, connection, TLS, server time, and response transfer.
Weeks 5-6
Failure reasoning

Practice slow dependencies, retry storms, proxy timeouts, resets, and DNS changes. Build an end-to-end deadline and retry policy for a read-only request, then explain why a write needs idempotency or reconciliation.
A troubleshooting checklist based on evidence and a diagram showing where each timeout is enforced.

lab.title: Estimate in-flight data and test framing
lab.scenario: A connection has a 100 Mb/s path and a 40 ms round-trip time. Separately, a local server sends a length-prefixed message in several writes. Use the examples to distinguish throughput constraints from application parsing.
steps: Convert units first: 100 million bits/second times 0.04 seconds is 4 million bits, about 500,000 bytes. This bandwidth-delay product estimates the data needed in flight to fill that idealized path, not guaranteed application throughput.

Send a four-byte length followed by a payload from your local server, splitting the payload across writes. The client must accumulate the header, validate a maximum length, and then collect exactly the declared payload bytes.

Disconnect the server before the payload completes. The client should return an incomplete-message error, not process truncated data or allocate unbounded memory. Repeat with two messages sent back-to-back.
lab.result: You can explain why available bandwidth, RTT, windowing, server behavior, and framing are separate concerns. The parser remains correct even when the transport delivers bytes in unexpected chunk sizes.
checks: Are bits and bytes converted consistently?
Does the client handle both fragmented and coalesced reads?
Are message size and total waiting time bounded?
lab.extension: Add a request ID and simulate losing the response after server processing. Explain why reconnecting and retrying a write can duplicate a business action even though TCP itself avoids duplicate bytes within one connection.

qa: Does UDP mean packets always arrive faster?

No. UDP provides datagrams without TCP's connection and reliability machinery, but applications still face loss, congestion, security, and ordering needs. Protocol choice depends on the desired semantics and workload.
Why can ping work while an API fails?

ICMP reachability does not prove DNS correctness, TCP port access, TLS validity, proxy behavior, or application health. Test the same path and protocol as the failing request before drawing a conclusion.
Is a timeout proof that the server did nothing?

No. The operation may have completed and its response may be delayed or lost. Reads can often be retried safely; side-effecting requests need a defined identity, status lookup, or reconciliation policy.
pitfalls: Assuming one socket read contains one complete application message.
Confusing receiver flow control with network congestion control.
Retrying every failed write with a fresh logical operation ID.
readiness: A browser request can be explained across protocol boundaries.
Partial reads and incomplete messages are handled correctly.
Timeouts are distinguished from known operation failure.
Measurements identify latency components instead of guessing.

title: Linux CLI and Debugging for Engineers
audience: Developers using Linux or WSL who want repeatable command-line workflows and a disciplined way to diagnose processes, files, permissions, and service failures.
summary: Treat the shell as a way to ask precise questions about a system. Learn navigation, quoting, streams, processes, logs, and debugging through a disposable local project. Prefer narrow read-only inspection before changing state, and preserve the evidence that supports each diagnosis.
outcomes: Use paths, quoting, pipelines, exit codes, and environment variables correctly.
Inspect a process's state, logs, open files, and listening endpoints.
Form and test a local debugging hypothesis with a minimal reproducer.
Avoid destructive troubleshooting and accidental exposure of secrets.
foundations: Commands have contracts

Understand arguments, standard input/output/error, exit status, and working directory. Quote paths containing spaces. A pipeline can hide an earlier failure unless the shell and script handle it deliberately; visible output alone is not proof of success.
Permissions are not a reason to escalate blindly

Inspect ownership, mode, path traversal permissions, and the actual user running a process. Broad permission changes or running everything as root can hide the cause and introduce risk. Fix the narrow ownership or access requirement instead.
Debug by discrimination

State what you expect, what happened, and one observation that distinguishes competing causes. A minimal reproducer reduces irrelevant state. Keep the original error and versions so another person can verify the result instead of relying on a vague narrative.
studyRule: Practice in a dedicated directory or disposable environment. Use read-only commands first, target only processes you own, and review any state-changing command before execution. Never paste credentials into a chat or a command history to get help.
plan: Week 1
Shell fundamentals
Learn navigation, quoting, redirection, pipes, environment scope, and exit codes. Create a small script that accepts a path, validates it, and reports useful errors. Test spaces and missing files.
A script that returns meaningful status and does not confuse filenames with shell syntax.
Week 2
Files and process state

Inspect file metadata, permissions, disk usage, process trees, CPU, memory, and local listening ports. Compare the environment of an interactive shell with a launched service. Learn graceful process termination before forced termination.
A checklist separating missing file, wrong working directory, permission failure, and port conflict.
Week 3
Logs and traces

Add structured timestamps and request IDs to a local service. Use its logs, a debugger, and authorized system-call tracing to inspect a failed request. Redact secrets and avoid collecting unrelated traffic.
One reproducible failure with a short evidence timeline and a confirmed controlling operation.
Week 4
Automation and recovery

Automate the reproducer and a regression test. Handle command failures explicitly and clean only resources created by the test. Document prerequisites and platform differences rather than assuming every Linux distribution has identical tools.
A repeatable diagnosis and fix that another engineer can run without manual guessing.

lab.title: Investigate a service that cannot open its configuration
lab.scenario: A program runs from your terminal but fails when launched as a service. The error says a configuration file is missing. Avoid changing permissions or copying files until you know which path is actually being opened.
steps: Record the process user, working directory, arguments, and configuration path. A relative path resolves against the process working directory, which may differ from the repository directory used interactively.

Use logs or a trace of the process you control to confirm the attempted file path and error. Inspect ownership and directory traversal permissions only after validating that the path is the intended one.

Pass an explicit configuration path or define a stable application-relative location. Add a test that launches from a different working directory and confirms the program either succeeds or reports a clear path error.
lab.result: The fix addresses the real environmental assumption rather than masking it with broad access changes. The regression test captures the difference between interactive and service execution.
checks: Does the observed attempted path support the hypothesis?
Is the fix limited to the application's configuration contract?
Does the error omit secret configuration values?
lab.extension: Repeat the exercise with a port already occupied by another local test process. Identify the owning process and choose an unused port instead of terminating unrelated services.

qa: Why did a command succeed but the script fail?
The script may use a different shell, environment, working directory, user, or quoting behavior. Compare those inputs and the exit status before assuming the tool itself is unreliable.
Should I use sudo to fix a permission error?

Only when elevated access is genuinely required and authorized. First inspect the path and ownership. Running the whole application with more privilege can create new files owned by root and make the original problem worse.
What makes a bug report useful?

Include expected and actual behavior, exact versions, a minimal reproducer, relevant sanitized output, and the smallest known conditions. Explain what you tested and what remains uncertain rather than providing only a screenshot of the final symptom.
pitfalls: Deleting caches or killing processes before preserving the failure evidence.
Using broad recursive permission changes as a default fix.
Leaking tokens through command history, screenshots, or debug logs.
readiness: Shell quoting and exit codes are understood.
A service failure can be reduced to a reproducible command.
Inspection precedes risky state changes.
A regression test verifies the actual root cause.

title: C and C++ Memory Safety Foundations
level: Basic C or C++ syntax required
audience: Engineers preparing for systems roles who need to reason about object lifetime, ownership, bounds, cleanup, and undefined behavior rather than rely on a program appearing to work once.
summary: Memory correctness is a contract about which object exists, who owns it, how it may be accessed, and when access ends. Learn these boundaries with small local programs, strong compiler warnings, sanitizers, and explicit cleanup reasoning. Keep C and C++ language rules distinct where they differ.
outcomes: Identify stack, heap, static-storage, and object-lifetime boundaries.
Document ownership transfer, borrowing, and cleanup for an API.
Use warnings and sanitizers to investigate bounds and lifetime defects.
Design error paths that release acquired resources exactly once.
foundations: Lifetime is more than an address

A pointer value can remain non-null after the referenced object's lifetime ends. Reusing the same address does not restore the old ownership contract. Define whether a function borrows data, copies it, or takes ownership, and how long the caller may retain a reference.
Bounds and representation matter

Track lengths and capacity separately. Account for terminators where required, check arithmetic before allocation, and avoid assuming serialized bytes are safely aligned native objects. Undefined behavior can invalidate reasoning even when a local run produces plausible output.
Use language tools appropriately

In modern C++, RAII and standard containers reduce manual cleanup, while smart pointers encode common ownership patterns. In C, explicit ownership conventions and structured cleanup are essential. Sanitizers find many bugs, but their absence does not prove correctness.
studyRule: Keep exercises small and run them with warnings and suitable debug instrumentation. Explain the ownership graph before optimizing. Use synthetic buffers and local programs; the objective is defensive correctness, not exploiting a deployed process.
plan: Week 1
Storage and lifetime

Trace local variables, dynamic allocations, returned values, and borrowed references. Write API comments that specify ownership and valid lifetime. Study copy, move, and destruction behavior if using C++.
A small ownership diagram and examples of safe return values versus invalid references to expired objects.
Week 2
Bounds and arithmetic

Practice buffers with explicit size and capacity, validated indexes, and checked allocation arithmetic. Test zero-length, maximum-size, and malformed input. Prefer standard containers where appropriate.
A parser or buffer utility with boundary tests and clear rejection of invalid sizes.
Week 3
Cleanup and errors

Exercise failures after each resource acquisition. In C, use a consistent cleanup path; in C++, use RAII objects with well-defined destruction. Ensure ownership is not duplicated during retries or partial initialization.
Tests showing every acquired resource is released once on success and each failure path.
Week 4
Concurrency and diagnosis

Study shared ownership, use-after-free risk across threads, and the distinction between atomic access and object lifetime. Use a debugger and sanitizers on local test cases, then explain the root cause and regression test.
A short diagnosis with the invalid lifetime transition and a minimal correction, not just a tool screenshot.

lab.title: Design a safe resource-loading API
lab.scenario: A function opens a file, allocates a buffer, parses metadata, and may fail at any stage. The caller needs a usable result on success and no leaked or dangling resources on failure.
steps: List resources and owners at each stage: file handle, allocated storage, parsed object, and any borrowed input. Specify whether the final object owns the buffer or copies data into separate storage.

Choose one cleanup strategy. In C++, wrap resources in RAII types; in C, initialize handles to safe states and route failures through ordered cleanup. Publish the result to the caller only after all required invariants hold.

Inject a failure after each acquisition and test invalid metadata, empty input, and allocation failure where your harness supports it. Verify no result points to temporary storage and no resource is released twice.
lab.result: Success returns an object with an explicit ownership contract, while every failure leaves the caller without partial ownership. The design remains understandable even before instrumentation is run.
checks: Does every resource have exactly one responsible owner?
Can the caller use the result after temporary parsing objects are destroyed?
Do instrumentation and manual lifetime reasoning agree?
lab.extension: Add asynchronous parsing and define how the input buffer remains alive until completion or cancellation. An atomic pointer alone is not a lifetime-management strategy.

qa: Does setting a pointer to null fix use-after-free?

It helps only for that pointer variable and does not invalidate other aliases. Correctness requires controlling ownership and access across all references, not merely clearing one local copy after freeing.
Is shared_ptr always the safest choice?

It can represent shared lifetime, but adds cost and can create cycles or hide unclear ownership. Prefer unique ownership when possible, and use weak references deliberately for non-owning relationships that must observe expiration.
Do sanitizers prove the program is safe?

No. They detect classes of defects on executed paths and within their instrumentation model. Combine them with tests, reviews, ownership contracts, and careful reasoning about unexecuted paths and concurrency.
pitfalls: Equating non-null pointers with live valid objects.
Ignoring integer overflow when computing allocation sizes.
Fixing a symptom without defining who owns the resource.
readiness: Ownership and borrowing are explicit in public interfaces.
Boundary and partial-initialization cases have tests.
Cleanup behavior is correct on every exit path.
A memory defect can be explained as a broken invariant.

title: Concurrency, Locks, and Safe Shutdown
audience: Developers preparing for multithreaded systems or backend roles who need to reason about shared state, coordination, contention, cancellation, and resource lifetime.
summary: Concurrency is about possible interleavings and invariants, not merely adding threads. Start with the state that must remain consistent, choose a synchronization boundary, and define shutdown before optimizing throughput. A correct steady-state loop can still fail during cancellation or partial initialization.
outcomes: Distinguish concurrency, parallel execution, atomicity, visibility, and ordering.
Write a bounded producer-consumer design with a clear protected predicate.
Recognize deadlock, starvation, contention, and unsafe lifetime transitions.
Test shutdown and failure paths instead of relying on timing sleeps.
foundations: Protect an invariant

A lock should guard a meaningful relationship, such as queue size and contents, rather than an arbitrary line of code. Reading two individually atomic fields can still observe an inconsistent combination if the invariant spans both. Define the valid state transitions first.
Waiting is conditional

A condition variable wakes a thread to recheck a predicate while holding the appropriate lock. It does not promise that the desired state remains true. Use a loop to handle spurious wakeups and competition from other threads.
Lifecycle is part of correctness

A worker may outlive the object that created it unless shutdown coordinates ownership. Stop accepting work, define drain or cancellation policy, wake waiters, join workers, and only then release resources they might still access.
studyRule: Prefer deterministic barriers, explicit state transitions, and targeted stress tests to arbitrary sleeps. Keep the first implementation simple with locks; introduce lock-free structures only when a measured bottleneck and expertise justify their additional proof obligations.
plan: Week 1
Races and invariants

Implement a shared counter and a two-field state transition. Explain why read-modify-write can race and why independent atomics may not preserve a compound invariant. Add the smallest synchronization boundary that establishes correctness.
A reproducible race demonstration and a corrected invariant with a clear happens-before argument.
Week 2
Queues and waiting
Build a bounded queue with not-empty and not-full predicates. Handle multiple producers and consumers. Validate capacity and ensure the lock is not held during the slow work itself.
Tests for empty waits, full waits, multiple workers, and preservation of every accepted item.
Week 3
Shutdown and cancellation
Add explicit closing state and decide whether queued work drains or is cancelled. Wake all affected waiters, reject new work, and join workers before destroying shared data.
A shutdown matrix covering empty, full, busy, and partially initialized states without hanging.
Week 4
Contention and design trade-offs
Measure lock hold time, throughput, and tail latency. Compare smaller critical sections, partitioned state, and batching before changing primitives. Review lock ordering and error paths.
A measured optimization that retains correctness and does not merely move the bottleneck elsewhere.

lab.title: Close a bounded queue without losing accepted work
lab.scenario: Several producers submit tasks to a capacity-limited queue and workers process them. The owner requests graceful shutdown while some producers are blocked on a full queue and some workers may be waiting for work.
steps: Under one lock, set a closing flag and stop accepting new submissions. Document whether a submission racing with close is accepted before the linearization point or rejected afterward. Never leave its result ambiguous.

Notify waiting producers so they can observe closure. Workers wait while the queue is empty and not closing; when closing and empty, they exit. When work remains, they remove it under the lock and process it outside the critical section.

Join all workers before freeing queue storage or callbacks they use. Count accepted and completed items, inject processing failures, and define how those failures are reported without deadlocking shutdown.
lab.result: The drain policy gives every accepted item a terminal outcome, and all waiters have an exit condition. Shared memory remains alive until workers stop referencing it.
checks: Does close wake producers as well as consumers?
Is each condition predicate rechecked in a loop?
Can destruction occur before any worker has finished using shared state?
lab.extension: Add immediate cancellation as a separate policy. Report cancelled queued items explicitly, distinguish them from in-flight work, and explain what can or cannot be interrupted safely.

qa: Does volatile make a shared counter thread-safe?

Not in C or C++. It does not provide the required atomic read-modify-write or general synchronization guarantees. Use the language's atomic or locking primitives according to the invariant and memory model.
Why not hold the queue lock during processing?
Slow processing would serialize unrelated producers and workers, increasing contention and tail latency. Remove or reserve the item under the lock, then perform independent work after releasing it.
Can more threads reduce throughput?

Yes. Contention, cache coherence, context switching, memory pressure, and dependency limits can outweigh parallelism. Measure the actual workload and resource bottleneck before increasing concurrency.
pitfalls: Using sleeps as the main correctness mechanism in concurrent tests.
Destroying shared resources before joining workers.
Assuming an atomic variable preserves a multi-variable invariant.
readiness: Each lock has a stated invariant and ownership rule.
Condition waits have explicit predicates and closure behavior.
Shutdown covers blocked, queued, and in-flight work.
Performance changes are measured without weakening correctness.

title: Databases, SQL, Indexes, and Transactions
duration: 4 weeks with a local relational database
audience: Backend and data-oriented engineers who can write simple queries but need to reason about data grain, constraints, indexing, isolation, and safe concurrent updates.
summary: A database is not just a place to store JSON. Its schema and transaction boundaries encode invariants, while indexes trade read efficiency for write and storage cost. Learn these decisions using a small order or reservation model and inspect actual query behavior.
outcomes: Define table grain, keys, constraints, and relationships before writing joins.
Use indexes based on predicates and access patterns rather than intuition alone.
Explain transaction isolation and concurrency failures with concrete examples.
Handle migrations, retries, and backups as part of the data lifecycle.
foundations: Grain prevents double counting

Know what one row represents in every table and intermediate result. Joining multiple one-to-many relationships can multiply rows. Aggregate at the correct key before combining measures, and use constraints to express identities that must be unique.
Indexes support workloads

An index can reduce lookup and ordering work when it matches the query, but it consumes space and must be maintained on writes. Inspect plans and representative row counts. A sequential scan can be correct and efficient for a small table or a broad query.
Transactions protect boundaries

Atomicity groups changes, while isolation defines what concurrent operations can observe. A read followed by a write does not automatically protect an invariant against another transaction. Constraints, conditional updates, locking, or stronger isolation may be necessary.
studyRule: Use PostgreSQL or another well-documented local database and synthetic data. Write the expected rows before running a query. For concurrency exercises, use two sessions and explicit steps instead of relying on chance timing.
plan: Week 1
Model and query

Build customers, orders, and items with primary and foreign keys. Practice joins, grouping, NULL behavior, and window functions. Test empty groups, duplicates, and ties rather than only clean sample data.
A schema diagram and queries whose output grain and edge cases are documented.
Week 2
Index and measure

Create a larger synthetic dataset and inspect query plans. Compare selective lookups, ordered history, and broad scans. Add a composite index for a real access pattern and measure read and write effects.
A before/after plan with workload size, query, and limitations; no unsupported claim that every index makes queries faster.
Week 3
Concurrent correctness

Use two sessions to reproduce a lost update or last-item reservation race. Add the database-enforced invariant and choose an appropriate transaction strategy. Test retry behavior after a conflict or ambiguous client timeout.
A deterministic concurrency test that never creates two owners for the same exclusive resource.
Week 4
Operational data changes
Practice a backward-compatible schema change, migration rollback or forward repair, backup, and restore in a disposable database. Explain which application versions can coexist during deployment.
A migration runbook and a tested restore, not merely a backup file whose recovery has never been attempted.

lab.title: Reserve the final seat safely
lab.scenario: Two clients try to reserve the last seat for an event. Both first read that the seat is available. The application must allow at most one active reservation, including when requests are retried.
steps: Model a stable seat/event identity and enforce a unique active ownership rule in the database. Define reservation states and whether an expired hold can be reclaimed. An application precheck alone is not the invariant boundary.

Perform the claim using an appropriate transaction or conditional update that succeeds only for the expected available state. Return a clear conflict when another transaction wins instead of silently overwriting ownership.

Run two sessions through the same interleaving, then retry the winning request with its original request ID. Verify one reservation and one logical result, and distinguish a known conflict from a timeout with an unknown outcome.
lab.result: Correctness comes from the database boundary and request identity, not from the timing of the availability check. The loser receives a defined result and retries do not create extra reservations.
checks: Can two concurrent claims violate the unique ownership rule?
Does retrying the same logical request preserve its result?
Are lock duration and transaction failure handled explicitly?
lab.extension: Add expiring holds and a payment callback. Describe what happens when payment succeeds after expiry; do not automatically confirm a seat that another customer now owns.

qa: Why not put an index on every column?

Indexes add write work, storage, and maintenance cost. Their usefulness depends on predicates, selectivity, ordering, and query shape. Choose them from measured workloads and inspect plans rather than indexing columns indiscriminately.
Does ACID mean every transaction is serializable?
No. Isolation levels differ, and a database's default may allow anomalies relevant to your invariant. Read the specific engine's contract and test the concurrency pattern you need to protect.
Why test restore if backups succeed?

A backup command can succeed while recovery assumptions, permissions, versions, or missing dependencies make restoration fail. A recovery plan is credible only after a representative restore and validation of the recovered data.
pitfalls: Joining child tables without checking row multiplication.
Using application checks instead of database-enforced invariants.
Claiming a backup strategy without a tested recovery path.
readiness: Schema keys and output grain are explicit.
Index choices are linked to observed access patterns.
Concurrent updates preserve the required invariant.
Migrations and restore procedures have been exercised.

title: Trace a Request Through DNS, TLS, and HTTP
duration: 2 weeks of browser and local-service labs
audience: Engineers who want a precise answer to 'what happens when you open a URL?' and a practical method for locating failures along that path.
summary: A browser request involves naming, connection selection, transport, server identity, HTTP semantics, intermediaries, and response rendering. The exact path depends on caches, existing connections, protocol versions, and proxies. Explain a concrete request rather than a memorized universal sequence.
outcomes: Separate DNS resolution, transport setup, TLS verification, and HTTP exchange.
Explain connection reuse, caches, redirects, and browser subresource requests.
Diagnose which stage contributes delay or failure using timing evidence.
Distinguish channel security from application authentication and authorization.
foundations: Naming is not connection

DNS maps names to records, often through caches with TTLs. A successful lookup does not prove the endpoint is reachable or healthy. Clients may try multiple addresses, reuse a connection, or interact through a proxy that changes the visible path.
TLS establishes a protected channel

Certificate validation and hostname checks help establish the expected server identity, while negotiated keys protect traffic. TLS does not automatically authorize an application user or make every returned document trustworthy. Avoid disabling verification as a troubleshooting shortcut.
HTTP has durable semantics across versions

Methods, status codes, headers, and cache rules remain important even when framing changes. HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over TCP; HTTP/3 uses QUIC. A redirect, conditional request, or cached response may avoid the simple full-fetch path.
studyRule: Choose one public page and one local API you control. Record the protocol and timing for each observation. Do not infer the internal architecture of a remote site from a single header, and do not capture private sessions or credentials.
plan: Days 1-3
Map naming and endpoints
Inspect the URL components, DNS records, cache behavior, and destination port. Compare a first request with a repeated request and explain which stages may be skipped or reused.
A labeled timeline that separates resolution from connection and does not assume every request performs fresh DNS.
Days 4-6
Understand transport and identity
Study TCP versus QUIC at the level needed to explain setup, loss, and streams. Inspect a valid certificate chain and hostname. Use a local test to observe connection refusal versus timeout.
An explanation of the failure stage and why bypassing certificate checks is not a valid permanent fix.
Days 7-10
Explore HTTP behavior

Implement a local endpoint with status codes, cache headers, and conditional requests. Observe redirects, request bodies, and response headers. Compare cache freshness with validation and understand that private content needs careful cache policy.
A repeatable trace showing a fresh response, a conditional validation, and the resulting client behavior.
Days 11-14
Diagnose end-to-end latency
Measure DNS, connection, TLS, server wait, and transfer time where the tool exposes them. Add a controlled server delay and a larger payload separately. Explain which metric changes and why.
A short troubleshooting report with observations, one hypothesis, a discriminating test, and a confirmed boundary.

lab.title: Explain a slow page without blaming the network
lab.scenario: A page loads slowly, but its HTML response is small. The browser also requests scripts, styles, images, and API data. You need to find whether the critical delay is resolution, connection, server work, transfer, or a dependent resource.
steps: Open the network timing view and identify the initial navigation plus dependent requests. Note cache status, connection reuse, and protocol. A fast HTML response does not mean the page is ready to render or interact.

Find the resource on the critical path and inspect its timing. Long server wait suggests a different investigation from a long download or blocked dependent request. Compare repeated observations instead of one noisy sample.

Reproduce the pattern locally by delaying an API or serving a large image. Change one variable and verify the expected timing component moves. Explain the evidence before recommending compression, caching, or backend optimization.
lab.result: The diagnosis identifies an actual stage and dependency rather than using 'network slow' as a catch-all. Optimization can then target a measured bottleneck and retain correct cache and security behavior.
checks: Were cached and uncached runs distinguished?
Does the proposed change affect the measured critical path?
Were credentials and private payloads excluded from shared traces?
lab.extension: Add an authenticated response and compare public versus private cache eligibility. Explain how an incorrect cache key could expose another user's content even over a perfectly valid TLS connection.

qa: Does HTTPS mean a site is trustworthy?

It protects the connection to the authenticated endpoint under the certificate model. It does not prove the site's claims are true, its application is safe, or the user is authorized for every resource.
Why does the second request often look faster?

DNS, connections, TLS sessions, and content may be cached or reused. Server and filesystem caches may also be warm. Identify which changed before treating the difference as a stable performance improvement.
Does HTTP/3 remove all head-of-line blocking?

It avoids TCP's cross-stream delivery blocking for independent QUIC streams, but application dependencies, stream-level ordering, congestion, and server scheduling can still delay work. Avoid turning one protocol improvement into a universal latency claim.
pitfalls: Describing every request as a fresh DNS plus TCP plus TLS handshake.
Disabling TLS verification to make an error disappear.
Treating time-to-first-byte as complete user-perceived page latency.
readiness: One real request can be explained with observed protocol details.
Naming, connection, identity, and application errors are distinguished.
Cache reuse and conditional validation can be demonstrated.
A latency recommendation follows a measured critical path.

title: Profile Performance and Explain Tail Latency
duration: 3 weeks using a repeatable local workload
audience: Developers who want to diagnose slow code or services using measurements rather than intuition, and communicate results without misleading averages or unsupported scalability claims.
summary: Performance work begins with a workload and a user-visible objective. Separate throughput, latency, resource consumption, and correctness. Measure a baseline, locate the dominant cost, change one thing, and verify both the improvement and its side effects under representative conditions.
outcomes: Define a reproducible benchmark with explicit inputs and resource limits.
Distinguish CPU work, blocking, allocation, storage, and queueing costs.
Interpret percentile latency and explain why averages can hide bad experiences.
Report improvements with method, variability, and remaining limitations.
foundations: Measure the right outcome

Requests per second, elapsed time, CPU time, memory, and p99 latency answer different questions. A batch task may prioritize completion time, while an interactive API needs a latency budget. Define the goal before selecting a profiler or optimization.
Workload shape matters

Dataset size, input distribution, concurrency, cache warmth, hardware, and dependency behavior can change the bottleneck. Record them. A synthetic hot-cache benchmark is not evidence of production performance under cold reads or burst traffic.
Queueing creates tails

As utilization approaches a bottleneck's capacity, waiting can grow sharply. Averages can conceal a small set of slow requests. Use enough samples, retain failures, and understand whether the load generator's behavior hides delays through coordinated omission.
studyRule: Keep benchmark code, configuration, and results together. Use a local service and bounded load. Repeat measurements, preserve failed requests, and validate correctness before accepting a faster result. Never stress a public or shared service without authorization.
plan: Days 1-4
Define and baseline

Choose one endpoint or algorithm, define the workload and latency goal, and collect elapsed time, throughput, errors, CPU, and memory. Record hardware and warm/cold conditions. Run repeated samples rather than one stopwatch measurement.
A baseline report that another engineer can reproduce and that includes error counts.
Days 5-8
Locate dominant work

Use CPU sampling, allocation data, traces, or blocked stacks as appropriate. Separate application execution from waits on locks, databases, or networks. Form a hypothesis that predicts a specific measurement change.
A profile or trace supporting one dominant cost and a proposed discriminating experiment.
Days 9-14
Make and test one change

Reduce repeated computation, improve a data structure, shrink a critical section, or avoid unnecessary I/O according to the evidence. Compare identical workloads and check correctness, memory, and tail behavior.
A before/after result with confidence limits or observed variability and no hidden workload changes.
Days 15-21
Check scaling and communicate

Vary concurrency and input size within safe limits. Identify saturation and trade-offs. Document what improved, what did not, and which production assumptions remain untested. Add a regression benchmark when stable enough.
A concise performance note with method, results, caveats, and the next likely bottleneck.

lab.title: A faster average but a worse user experience
lab.scenario: Batching database writes improves average throughput, but some requests wait much longer. The service flushes only when the batch is full, so low-traffic requests can sit indefinitely without a maximum wait.
steps: Measure latency distribution at both low and high arrival rates. Include requests that timed out. Separate time waiting for a batch from time executing the database write, and compare the result with the original non-batched path.

Introduce a bounded flush interval in addition to the maximum batch size. State whether deadlines can force an earlier flush and how backpressure works when the database slows. Keep the queue itself bounded.
Repeat the same workloads and compare throughput, p50, p95, p99, errors, and memory. Verify that shutdown flushes or explicitly fails pending work rather than losing accepted requests.
lab.result: The revised design balances throughput with a documented waiting bound. An optimization is accepted only if it meets the service objective and preserves correctness, not merely because one average improved.
checks: Does the low-traffic case complete within the intended budget?
Are timed-out and failed requests included in the report?
Is memory bounded when the downstream service is slower than ingress?
lab.extension: Add a burst followed by quiet traffic and inspect the final partial batch. Explain why testing only steady maximum load would miss this latency defect.

qa: Why not optimize the function that looks inefficient?

It may contribute little to the end-to-end cost. A profile and workload determine where time or resources are actually spent. Optimize the controlling bottleneck, then remeasure because the bottleneck may move.
Can I average p99 values from several servers?

Not to obtain a valid global p99 in general. Percentiles are not directly additive or averageable. Merge compatible distributions or use an aggregation method that preserves the required sample information.
Does lower CPU mean the service improved?
Not necessarily. It may be blocked longer, doing less work, or dropping requests. Interpret CPU alongside throughput, latency, errors, and the correctness of completed results.
pitfalls: Changing dataset or cache state between baseline and optimized runs.
Reporting only averages and omitting errors or timeouts.
Improving throughput by allowing unbounded queues and memory growth.
readiness: A workload and objective are explicit and reproducible.
The proposed optimization follows measured evidence.
Tail latency and errors are part of the comparison.
Results include limitations and correctness checks.

title: Git, Code Review, and CI That Protect Changes
duration: 3 weeks on a small personal repository
audience: Developers who can commit code but want safer collaboration, reviewable changes, meaningful automated checks, and an understandable recovery workflow.
summary: Version control records decisions; code review checks risk and clarity; CI verifies repeatable contracts. Use all three together. A green pipeline is not proof of correctness, and a large commit message cannot compensate for an unreviewable change that mixes unrelated behavior.
outcomes: Inspect and preserve local and remote changes before editing or publishing.
Create small coherent commits and review descriptions grounded in behavior.
Build CI checks that test meaningful risks and fail clearly.
Recover through safe reversible operations instead of destructive guessing.
foundations: Understand the three states

Working files, the staging area, and committed history are different. Inspect status and diffs before committing. Fetching updates remote-tracking information; it does not by itself integrate another person's changes into your working branch.
Review the behavioral contract

Explain what changed, why, and how it was checked. A reviewer needs the relevant assumptions, failure cases, and compatibility risks. Keep refactoring separate from behavior changes when that improves reviewability rather than obscuring causality.
CI is executable agreement

Run formatting or linting, focused tests, and build checks appropriate to the project. Use reproducible dependency versions and avoid secrets in logs. Tests should fail on a real broken condition, not merely execute code without asserting behavior.
studyRule: Practice on a repository you own with a small feature and regression test. Do not rewrite shared history without agreement. When a worktree contains changes you did not make, preserve them and understand their relationship to your task.
plan: Week 1
State and history

Practice status, diff, staging, commit, log, branches, fetch, and merge using disposable examples. Introduce a conflicting edit and resolve it by understanding both changes rather than selecting one side blindly.
A small history whose commits each have one purpose and whose conflict resolution preserves both intended behaviors.
Week 2
Review and regression tests

Make a narrow bug fix with a test that fails before the fix and passes afterward. Write a review description covering cause, behavior, validation, and residual risk. Review another small change for edge cases.
A reviewable patch and a regression test that demonstrates the failure mechanism.
Week 3
Automate and recover

Add CI for the agreed checks and test it on a deliberately failing branch. Practice reverting a published change with a new commit. Document release and rollback steps and avoid relying on a local-only environment.
A pipeline that catches the known regression and a recovery exercise that preserves shared history.
Ongoing
Keep feedback useful

Remove flaky assumptions, keep test fixtures deterministic, and record why a check exists. Review dependency updates and permissions. Prefer a small set of trustworthy gates over many ignored red builds.
A maintained checklist linking each required gate to a meaningful project risk.

lab.title: Fix a bug while preserving another contributor's work
lab.scenario: Your local repository is clean, but the remote branch has gained changes since your last fetch. You need to publish a small fix without discarding a newer feature or forcing an overwrite.
steps: Fetch and inspect the remote difference before editing or integrating. Identify whether the newer changes affect the same contract. A clean status relative to stale tracking information does not prove the remote is unchanged.

Create a focused fix and a regression test. Integrate remote work using the team's agreed merge or rebase workflow, resolving conflicts from behavior rather than file ownership. Rerun the focused check after integration.

Push without force when possible and inspect the actual CI or deployment result. Verify the intended version, then report what was checked and any remaining uncertainty instead of equating a successful push with a successful release.
lab.result: The fix and the other contributor's feature remain intact, the regression is covered, and publication is verified. The process protects both history and behavior.
checks: Was the remote state refreshed before publication?
Does the conflict resolution preserve both intended changes?
Did the deployment verify the exact commit rather than an older successful run?
lab.extension: Simulate a deployment regression and use a revert commit or the documented rollback mechanism. Explain why deleting local files or resetting shared history is not a substitute for a controlled recovery.

qa: Is a green CI run enough to approve a change?

No. It verifies only the checks that ran under their assumptions. Review design, edge cases, security, and compatibility, and state untested risks. A test suite can be green while missing the changed contract entirely.
Should every change be one commit?

A commit should represent a coherent step that can be understood and, ideally, tested. Several focused commits may be better than one enormous change; many arbitrary fragments may be worse. Follow the team's review conventions.
When is force-pushing appropriate?

Only within an agreed workflow and with care for shared work. It rewrites remote history and can disrupt others. Prefer non-destructive integration and obtain approval before rewriting a shared branch.
pitfalls: Publishing against stale remote-tracking information.
Resolving conflicts by discarding unfamiliar changes.
Treating lint or coverage percentage as proof of behavioral correctness.
readiness: Working, staged, committed, and remote states are understood.
A regression test demonstrates the bug being fixed.
Review descriptions identify risks and verification.
Release and rollback steps have been exercised safely.

title: Distributed Systems from First Principles
audience: Engineers who know APIs and databases and want to understand replication, consistency, partitions, retries, and coordination without relying on slogans.
summary: A distributed system contains independently failing components that communicate with uncertain delays. Correct design states what remains true during retries, crashes, and partitions. Start from invariants and failure boundaries, then select replication and coordination mechanisms that support the promised behavior.
outcomes: Distinguish local failure, communication failure, and an unknown operation outcome.
Explain consistency choices in terms of user-visible reads and writes.
Design idempotent processing with durable identities and bounded retries.
Reason about leadership, fencing, replication, and recovery without claiming universal exactly-once behavior.
foundations: A timeout is ambiguous

The remote operation may not have started, may still be running, or may have completed with a lost response. The client cannot infer which solely from elapsed time. Durable operation identity and status reconciliation make retries safer.
Consistency is a contract

Describe which writes a read must observe and under what failure conditions. Eventual convergence, read-your-writes, and linearizable operations have different costs and guarantees. Do not choose a database category as a substitute for stating the needed semantics.
Ownership must survive failures

A lease can expire while a paused worker later resumes. A fencing token or generation checked by the protected resource can prevent stale owners from committing. Merely believing that a new leader exists does not stop an old process from acting.
studyRule: For every design, trace success, lost response, duplicate delivery, process crash, and partition. State the durable boundary and what a client can safely retry. Use a small local simulation before studying a larger product's architecture.
plan: Week 1
Failures and identities

Study RPC timeouts, retries, idempotency keys, backoff, and deadlines. Build a request table that stores a logical operation's status and result. Test duplicate requests with identical and conflicting payloads.
A retry contract that distinguishes safe replay from a new business action.
Week 2
Replication and reads

Compare leader-based replication, asynchronous replicas, and quorum concepts. Describe stale reads and failover behavior. Learn that replication does not replace backups or protect against every correlated failure.
A read/write timeline with explicit consistency and data-loss assumptions.
Weeks 3-4
Coordination and recovery
Study logs, consensus at a conceptual level, leases, epochs, and fencing. Analyze a paused worker that resumes after replacement. Add durable checkpoints and replay to a simple job processor.
A recovery scenario where stale work cannot overwrite the current owner's result.
Weeks 5-6
Operate the system

Add bounded queues, backpressure, observability, and failure injection. Define service-level goals, recovery objectives, and a runbook. Evaluate which guarantees remain possible during a network partition.
A design note with invariants, failure matrix, capacity limits, and a tested recovery path.

lab.title: A job finishes, but its acknowledgement is lost
lab.scenario: A worker updates a database and crashes before acknowledging its queue message. The broker later redelivers the same job. The system must avoid applying a business effect twice.
steps: Give the job a stable ID. In the same database transaction as the business update, record that the job has been applied, using a uniqueness constraint. If the transaction never commits, redelivery can safely attempt it again.
On redelivery, inspect the durable job record and return the stored outcome rather than repeating the effect. Acknowledge only after the transaction reaches the promised durable boundary.

If the effect is an external API call rather than a local transaction, preserve a provider idempotency key and reconcile ambiguous outcomes. Do not claim that the database deduplication record atomically controls an unrelated remote service.
lab.result: The local database effect is deduplicated under the stated transaction contract. External effects require their own coordination or reconciliation strategy; the design names that boundary instead of hiding it under 'exactly once.'
checks: Is the deduplication record committed with the local effect?
Can the same job ID be reused with a different payload?
What happens when the acknowledgement or provider response is lost?
lab.extension: Add a worker lease and simulate a long pause. Require the destination to check a monotonically increasing fencing value before accepting a write from a resumed stale worker.

qa: Does replication guarantee no data loss?

Only within its stated durability, acknowledgement, and failure model. Asynchronous replicas can lag, and correlated failures or logical corruption can affect all copies. Explain the recovery-point objective and backup strategy separately.
Does CAP mean choose any two forever?

That slogan is misleading. During a partition, a system cannot simultaneously provide the relevant strong consistency and availability guarantees for every operation. Discuss the operation, failure conditions, and actual contract rather than assigning one permanent label.
Is exactly-once delivery the same as exactly-once effect?

No. Delivery, processing, and an external business effect are different boundaries. Transactions and deduplication can establish useful scoped guarantees, but each destination and retention window must be considered explicitly.
pitfalls: Treating a timeout as evidence that nothing happened.
Using leases without preventing stale owners from writing.
Promising end-to-end exactly-once effects from a queue setting alone.
readiness: Every important operation has a named invariant.
Retries preserve a durable logical identity.
Read consistency and failure behavior are explicit.
Recovery tests cover lost responses and stale workers.
